extracted.intended_audience: educators, philosophers of education, teachers, and students of educational theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria and practical standards from John Dewey's Democracy and Education for judging or designing educative practices, institutions, and environments. Focuses on what counts as genuine education vs. mere training and how social and formal mechanisms should function to foster growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as social transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the means of social continuity: transmission of the group's interests, purposes, information, skill, and practices from mature to immature members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate effort and taking of thoughtful pains are required; mere physical growth or subsistence is insufficient. Without this transmission a group's characteristic life will cease. Example emphasis: the immature must be 'rendered cognizant of' and 'actively interested' in social aims and habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as communication (shared understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine education secures a common understanding via communication that creates similar emotional and intellectual dispositions—'like-mindedness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication modifies both parties; to communicate fully one must 'formulate' experience so another can appreciate its meaning. Social life 'exists in transmission, in communication' and therefore is educative when it creates shared aims, beliefs, and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of informal (incidental) and formal (intentional) education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education includes both incidental learning through living with others and deliberate schooling; maintaining a proper balance between these modes is a central problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools are one important but relatively superficial means; overreliance on formal methods risks loss of vitality. The task: place scholastic methods in true context by preserving connections to everyday social experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of abstract, remote, or 'dead' formal instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal instruction must not become remote, dead, or merely 'bookish'—isolated from the subject matter of life-experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subject matter remains technical and symbolic without being assimilated into lived activity, schooling creates 'egoistic specialists' and 'sharps' in learning. Anti-patterns: teaching as conveying isolated facts or symbols with no practical connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should make learners partners in shared activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The social medium is educative when it makes the immature a sharer or partner in common activities so they feel the group's successes and failures as their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely arranging stimuli to produce desired acts (training) is insufficient; participation that arouses the same ideas and emotions as the group leads to internalization of beliefs and knowledge. Example contrast: horse trained for tasks vs. a human child who becomes a copartner and shares aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between training and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Training alters outer habitual actions (automatic responses) while education changes mental and emotional dispositions, converting action into meaningful, socially shared purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training may yield automatic competence without understanding (e.g., dodging a blow), whereas education requires that actions be rooted in shared purposes, leading to corresponding beliefs and feelings. Beware systems that only condition behavior without developing understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment as formative (conditions of growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The environment consists of conditions that promote or hinder characteristic activities; it educates by calling out certain responses and shaping disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An educative environment aligns with the actor's active tendencies—what 'enters into this activity as a sustaining or frustrating condition.' Evaluate environments by how they stimulate desirable activities and inhibit counterproductive ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of language must connect to shared experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Language acquires meaning through joint activity; words must be tied to shared actions or imaginative participation to convey understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sound like 'hat' only becomes meaningful when used within a shared activity (e.g., mother putting hat on child). Teaching by words alone, without imaginative or experiential connection, reduces language to mere stimulus with no intellectual value (e.g., arithmetic symbols as rote stimuli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should foster interest and active engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Education must make learners actively interested, not merely subjects of external control; interests motivate assimilation of knowledge into practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared activities and environments that arouse and strengthen certain impulses lead to fuller participation; when learners lack interest, learning is shallow. Evaluate methods by their capacity to create authentic interest tied to social participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions judged by their effect on quality of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The worth of social institutions (economic, domestic, political, legal, religious) is measured by their contribution to enlarging and improving conscious experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This educative effect should be an important purpose in institutions, particularly through dealings with the young; curricula and institutional practices should be assessed on how they improve the quality of experience, not solely on external outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of symbolic knowledge with practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge stored in symbols must be translated into familiar acts or practical meaning; otherwise it remains artificial and unassimilated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As civilizations advance much knowledge is technical/symbolic—formal education must connect such material to lived experience (avoid making school subject-matter 'isolated from the subject matter of life-experience').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent split between conscious knowledge and absorbed character
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should avoid creating a split between what is learned consciously (specific instruction) and what is unconsciously absorbed in character through association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for education that integrates deliberate instruction with formation of disposition so that consciously acquired knowledge informs character and vice versa; evaluate programs by their coherence across these dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social environment shapes aims, attention, and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: The social medium determines objects of esteem and aversion, prescribing directions and limits of observation and memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a social or classroom environment directs attention towards socially valued objects and activities and thereby cultivates corresponding memory and judgment, rather than leaving learners' attentional habits unguided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education requires imaginative rehearsal for remote subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct shared action is impossible (e.g., learning history or remote artifacts), education must use imaginative participation to make remote subjects present and meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pedagogies of distant or historical content by their capacity to enable learners to 'rehearse imaginatively' the activities in which those objects had use, so words and descriptions elicit participatory understanding rather than mere factual acquaintance.
